ASTRA · AUTOMATED PRELIMINARY INSIGHTS
Does adding Fibonacci information help locate OXTR binding regions?

Not yet demonstrated. This OXTR pilot found no clear prediction benefit from adding Fibonacci and Phi Ratio features. It did not test biological prediction using M9 P24 Alpha, Beta, Gamma or Epsilon. The evidence concerns CTCF, one DNA-binding protein, in one stem-cell context—not transcription factors generally. This is an automated preliminary report; Gemini oversight is deferred.

What the agent completed

The agent completed a classical comparison of ordinary DNA binding-pattern and spacing features with and without Fibonacci/Phi Ratio features. It learned on chromosome 1, chose the model on chromosome 2, and tested OXTR on chromosome 3: it never saw OXTR laboratory answers while learning or choosing. Separately, the agent prepared a new matched pair of DNA windows, one overlapping a reported CTCF peak and one nearby comparison window, compiled all eight representations for each, and completed 16 local CUDA-Q CPU checks. The eight preparations are the same DNA represented as ordinary, Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Epsilon and shuffled controls.

What this means for your question

Average precision rose from 0.0719 to 0.0739. This is a ranking score, not percent accuracy. The estimated change was 0.0020, with a 95% uncertainty range from −0.0263 to 0.0082: it spans harm and benefit, so the outcome is inconclusive. The small pilot and laboratory quality warnings limit confidence. Saved CUDA-Q/Aquila readings describe the programmed system, not binding probabilities; the two saved DNA samples do not overlap the reported CTCF peaks. Those readings do not support binding prediction, and noisy changes do not establish benefit.

Where this run stops

The newly prepared pair checks the programs; it does not validate prediction. A larger quantum prediction test needs more matched quantum measurements covering reported binding and comparison regions, and a larger independent biological test remains necessary. Today’s instruction prohibits new Aquila submissions; none were made, and no new quantum hardware jobs were submitted. Future Aquila submission requires fresh device validation and explicit allowance; paid qBraid execution also lacks a new credit allowance. The completed pair preparation and local checks need no repeat.

The comparison, in plain numbers

CTCF is one protein that binds DNA. We checked whether each method ranked the eight OXTR windows overlapping reported CTCF regions above the other 144 windows. The laboratory map contains five peak regions; some span more than one window.

Average precision is a ranking score from 0 to 1. Higher is better; it is not percentage accuracy.
Method	OXTR ranking score
DNA motif and spacing features	0.0719
Same features + Fibonacci spacing and Phi Ratio	0.0739

Change: 0.0020. The 95% interval from resampling DNA blocks runs from -0.0263 to 0.0082. An interval spanning zero leaves the benefit unresolved.

How the saved quantum work fits

The agent reused all 16 CUDA-Q simulations and 16 Aquila measurements, covering two DNA samples prepared with ordinary input, Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Epsilon and a shuffled control. Those two samples contain no reported CTCF peak. They establish measured quantum responses, but this set alone cannot compare binding regions with non-binding regions. The new prediction scores above come from classical calculations.

The next quantum test is already prepared

The agent selected one OXTR DNA window overlapping a reported CTCF region and one nearby comparison window. It compiled all eight representations for each and checked all 16 programs with CUDA-Q on the local CPU. These are new local simulations; the qBraid GPU and Aquila readings above are the saved earlier measurements. No new cloud quantum job was submitted. Two windows check the programs; a larger set is necessary to assess prediction.
